name: Iris Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for agreeing to this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenline, a four-person agency that does labels and packaging for local food producers: jam, cheese, a couple of small breweries. A normal day is fixing label layouts so the ingredients list fits, checking barcodes, and sending files to Mercer Print across town. Graham, the owner, does the client meetings and the clever ideas. I do the careful bits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the day a new label comes back from the printer and it's on a real jar. I'm not the most creative person, Graham says my first drafts are safe, but I'm good at spotting when a colour's wrong on a proof. What wears me down is the redrafts, when a cheesemaker changes the weight on the label for the fourth time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get excited about every new thing, and most of it calms down. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, but fine isn't the same as safe when your little label agency lives on about twelve food clients. If two of them go bust, Graham can't keep four of us. I've got about three months saved, which isn't much if that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd try to get quicker at the redrafts and keep my savings growing a little each month. I wouldn't touch the AI tools, because I don't see why I'd need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, the way I always am. Small food firms close all the time, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Greenline is small. How steady is the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes up and down with the seasons, busy before Christmas and before summer markets. Last spring Graham cut us to four days for six weeks, and nobody said a word, because we all knew why. It came back, but it reminded me how thin it all is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Daniel do with money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We keep separate accounts and split the bills. My partner Daniel supervises shifts at the supermarket depot, so his pay is steadier than mine. We're careful, we cook at home, we take one holiday a year.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because new things always calm down.
I wouldn't post anything, because I **don't really post**.
think: Fine isn't the same as **safe** at a four-person agency.
Losing two of **twelve food clients** would cost Greenline a job.
do: Carry on and get quicker at **label redrafts**.
Grow her **three months** of savings a little each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, as always, because small food firms close all the time.
S0.quote: Fine isn't the same as safe when your little label agency lives on about twelve food clients.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: **seasonal work** and short weeks last spring.
She has **no interest** in AI tools in this world.
Daniel's **depot job** is the steadier household income.

steps.text: Keep fixing labels and checking proofs at Greenline
Add a little to her three months of savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business. If a tool can lay out an ingredients list in ten seconds, food companies will use it, and you can't really blame them. I'd keep my opinions fairly quiet at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is the kind that goes. Fitting text on labels, checking barcodes, resizing for different jar sizes, all of that is exactly what these tools are for. Graham would keep the ideas person, which is him, and maybe one designer who's quick with the software, and that isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham straight out whether there's a place for me in a year. I'd start saving harder, maybe an extra hundred a month by cutting the takeaways and the gym. And I'd ask Sofia at Mercer Print whether they ever train people for the press side, because I already know proofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like change, and this is change coming at me whether I like it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Graham might bring in the tools. How would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but I'd try if Graham asked, because I'd rather learn it than be shown the door. I'm slow with new software, it took me a year to feel comfortable in the layout program. So I'd be learning it while worrying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of your job that feels safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The proof checking, maybe, because it happens at the printer with real paper and real ink. You have to hold it under the light and see the green's gone muddy. That's why I keep thinking about Mercer Print.

say: I'd say it's **business**, and food firms will use a faster tool.
I'd keep my **opinions quiet** at work.
think: Fitting text, checking barcodes and resizing are **exactly what tools do**.
Graham would keep himself and **one quick designer**, and that isn't me.
do: Ask Graham directly whether there's **a place for her** in a year.
Save **an extra 100** a month by cutting takeaways and the gym.
Ask Sofia at Mercer Print about **press-side training**.
feel: **Anxious**, because change is coming whether she likes it or not.
S1.quote: Fitting text on labels, checking barcodes, resizing for different jar sizes, all of that is exactly what these tools are for.
fieldNote: She blames **no one**: food firms choosing cheaper tools is just business.
Her one hands-on skill, **checking proofs**, points her toward the printer.
She'd learn tools **reluctantly**, slowly and while worried.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and cut takeaways
Ask Sofia at Mercer Print about training for the press side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say very little, to be honest. Maybe that the government should do something, but I wouldn't know what. I'd mostly be asking people if they've heard of any jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Greenline closes or shrinks to Graham alone by 2028. Labels are pure screen work, there's nothing for a robot to wait for. I'd be out of a job before I'd even worked out what to do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back to the basics and stop any holidays. I'd go to Mercer Print and ask for anything on the press floor, even nights. And I'd sit down with Daniel and work out how long his pay can carry both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'm not someone who jumps, and losing my design job in two years would push me off a ledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's pay would cover rent and food, just about, but nothing else. We'd stop saving for a deposit, which we've been doing for two years. I'd feel awful about him carrying me, even though he'd never say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the printing work last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit longer. Mercer Print still needs people to load the machines and check the colours until robots can do that, maybe 2031. But the depot where Daniel works is hands-on too, so in a few years we could both be in the same boat.

say: I'd say **very little**, maybe that the government should act.
I'd mostly be asking people about **any jobs** going.
think: Greenline **closes or shrinks** to Graham alone by 2028.
Labels are **pure screen work**, so there's no robot delay to wait for.
do: Cut back to **basics** and stop holidays.
Ask Mercer Print for any **press-floor work**, even nights.
Work out with Daniel how long **his pay** carries them both.
feel: **Frightened**, like being pushed off a ledge by someone who never jumps.
S2.quote: I'm not someone who jumps, and losing my design job in two years would push me off a ledge.
fieldNote: She sees the **robot delay** helping printing and Daniel's depot, but only until about 2031.
The couple would stop saving for a **house deposit**.
She feels **guilty** about Daniel carrying her.

steps.text: Cut spending to basics and cancel this year's holiday
Apply for press-floor work at Mercer Print, including nights
Rely on Daniel's depot pay for rent and food
Pause saving for the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so people should be practical and learn something steady. I'd tell my younger cousin to think twice about design college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I still lose the design job, maybe around 2030. The difference is I'd have time to train at the printer before it happens, instead of begging for nights. But the printer has its own clock, robots by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Sofia whether I could do a day a week at Mercer Print, learning the press, while staying at Greenline four days. I'd keep saving an extra hundred a month. Daniel and I would keep the deposit savings but buy something smaller, or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, under a calm face. I'm a planner, so having a plan helps, but the plan only buys a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change whether you learn the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, because Graham would make me. I'd learn just enough to keep my job while I train at the printer. I'm not going to become a tools person, that's not who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Daniel think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's practical, like me. My partner Daniel thinks his depot will have robots before most places, so we're both looking at the same few years. He keeps saying we should have one of us in something boring and safe, like a council job.

say: I'd say people should be **practical** and learn something steady.
I'd tell my cousin to **think twice** about design college.
think: I still lose the design job, maybe **around 2030**.
Five years buys **printer training**, but robots arrive there by 2034.
do: Ask for **one day a week** learning the press at Mercer Print.
Shrink or delay the **house deposit** plans with Daniel.
feel: **Alarmed** under a calm face, because the plan only buys a few years.
S3.quote: My partner Daniel thinks his depot will have robots before most places, so we're both looking at the same few years.
fieldNote: Both household jobs face the **robot clock**, a shared risk she sees clearly.
She would learn AI only **enough to stay**.
Advising her cousin away from **design college** shows how she sees the field.

steps.text: Spend one day a week learning the press at Mercer Print
Keep saving an extra 100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should panic. People should just start moving in good time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to change jobs properly, but I know myself. I'd probably wait until about 2030 and then rush. Still, it's a lot better than two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Greenline, keep saving, and maybe do a course in print production in the evenings when it felt right. I'd wait to see what happens to other agencies before quitting anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere between uneasy and anxious. It's still going to happen, I just don't have to look at it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound more settled. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled, but not settled. I'd still be losing the design job at some point, and I'd be thirty-seven and starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you choose to do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something like a council print room or a school's print shop, steady and boring. I'd rather have boring and safe than exciting and gone.

People should start **moving in good time**.
think: Ten years is enough, but I'd probably **wait until 2030** and then rush.
I'd still be **starting over** at thirty-seven.
do: Take an evening **print production** course when it feels right.
feel: Between **uneasy and anxious**, without having to look at it every day.
S4.quote: I'd rather have boring and safe than exciting and gone.
fieldNote: Her ideal is **boring and safe**, like a council print room.
Ten years softens the fear but **doesn't remove** it.

steps.text: Stay at Greenline doing labels and proofs
Watch what happens to other agencies before quitting
Take an evening print production course later in the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and that one doesn't let you be slow. What would help is someone telling me plainly which jobs will still exist, and paid training for those jobs. I don't need a speech, I need a list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the food producers. The jam lady and the cheesemaker are lovely, and they'll use whatever's cheapest because they barely make a profit. Nobody's the villain in my version of AI, it's just everyone being careful with money.

headlineQuote: Nobody's the villain in my version of AI, it's just everyone being careful with money.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Greenline, a four-person label and packaging agency.
She **never uses AI tools**, plans carefully and lives with Daniel, a depot supervisor.
Her **pragmatic views** mean she blames nobody, seeing cheaper tools as ordinary business.
Her escape route is **press work** at Mercer Print, which only buys a few years.
She admits she would **wait too long** even with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it gives a slow changer no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **plain list** of jobs that will still exist, with **paid training** for them.
